why_this_might_be_wrong: I am fairly confident the directional effects are gone - two Fed-authored retractions covering exactly our window is unusually clean evidence. The way I could be wrong is in the other direction: by treating 'disappeared on average since 2021' as 'never present', when both papers describe an average over a period that includes regimes. The honest position is that our sample cannot distinguish these hypotheses at all, and the correct action is to record that and move on rather than to spend trials on it. I include this entry mainly so that the retraction papers are on file: the pre-FOMC drift is exactly the kind of famous, well-cited, Fed-branded result that an unattended agent would otherwise rediscover and act on.

name: Price discovery has migrated to the closing auction, and our session ends fifteen minutes before it
source_claim: Bogousslavsky and Muravyev (Journal of Financial Markets 2023) document that closing auctions grew from 3.1% of US equity daily volume in 2010 to 7.5% in 2018, that volume migrates 'not just to the end of the trading day but to the last five minutes and especially the auction', that the 15:30-15:55 share of volume DECLINED over the same period, and that 'as volume migrates towards the close, liquidity at the open deteriorates'. Industry data puts closing auctions at 9.44% of total US equity notional and $55.5bn/day in Q2 2024, both records. They also find auctions 'match volumes at low cost with lower price impact than during continuous trading, and auction price deviations revert quickly and almost completely, on average'. The driver is structural: index funds and ETFs must transact at the official closing price used for NAV.

sources.title: Who trades at the close? Implications for price discovery and liquidity
sources.author_or_org: Vincent Bogousslavsky, Dmitriy Muravyev (Journal of Financial Markets)
sources.what_it_measured: Closing auction volume share 2010-2018, its composition by trader type, price impact versus continuous trading, and the reversion of auction price deviations.

sources.title: NYSE Closing Auction: price discovery opportunities reach new highs
sources.author_or_org: NYSE (Intercontinental Exchange)
sources.what_it_measured: Closing auction notional and share of consolidated volume, reported at record levels.

sources.title: Closing time: How passive investing is reshaping equity market microstructure
sources.author_or_org: State Street Global Advisors
sources.what_it_measured: The mechanism linking index/ETF NAV calculation to closing-auction concentration.

contradictory_evidence: Bogousslavsky and Muravyev themselves supply the caution that matters: auction price deviations 'revert quickly and almost completely', so the auction is not systematically mispriced and there is no free drift to collect from it. This is a claim about WHERE liquidity and price discovery are, not a claim that either is exploitable. Separately, all of this evidence concerns CASH EQUITIES; the transmission to index futures between 15:45 and 16:00 is our inference and no source I found measures it. And the lab's own journal already reports that the last half hour is where the sign 'leans against the day's move' and calls it 'a pure cost refusal: there is no gross there to buy in either direction' - a direct internal warning against expecting anything tradeable in the closing window.
our_inference: We infer a question about the lab's own session convention rather than a strategy. The runner flattens at 15:45. The economically focal price of the day is set at 16:00, and an increasing share of the day's genuine information-bearing flow now transacts in the last five minutes and the auction. We infer two consequences worth measuring. (1) The 15:45 flatten may be systematically selling into, or buying into, the hedging flow that precedes the auction - which is a COST question (what is our realised slippage in the 15:40-15:45 window relative to the rest of the session?) rather than an alpha question. (2) The 15:45-16:00 futures window may carry a measurable relationship to the auction imbalance, and if the direction of that flow were estimable it would be a once-a-day, very short-horizon trade. We flag (2) as almost certainly beyond our data.
proposed_mechanism: Index and ETF funds must trade at the official close, so their demand is inelastic with respect to price and known in aggregate only through the exchange imbalance feeds published from 15:50. Liquidity providers who intend to supply the auction hedge in the futures beforehand, because the futures are the cheapest instrument in which to warehouse index risk. That hedging is a predictable, non-information-bearing flow in ES and NQ in the final minutes - which is exactly the type of flow PD-09's framework says should displace price temporarily and revert.
observable_variables: ret_1545_1600 = close(16:00) / close(15:45) - 1 in ES and NQ, available because the store holds full Globex bars past the cash close
volume profile of the final 30 minutes relative to the session, per instrument, and its trend across the sample
ES spread in each of the final 15 minutes from ES_quotes.parquet, versus the session median (the PD-02 link, and the most directly actionable measurement here)
relation of ret_1545_1600 to the day's return, to the 15:00-15:45 return, and to relative volume
reversion: ret_1600_next0930 conditioned on ret_1545_1600, testing whether the closing displacement reverts overnight
failure_conditions: The alpha reading fails - and I expect it to - if ret_1545_1600 has no relationship to any observable we hold, which is likely because the auction imbalance is the driving variable and we cannot see it. The COST reading fails only if ES spread in the final 15 minutes is indistinguishable from the session median, which would contradict both the U-shape literature and PD-02.
data_we_lack: The closing auction imbalance feed (NYSE and Nasdaq publish indicative imbalances from 15:50), and the official closing prices themselves. Without the imbalance we have the flow's footprint but not its sign or size, which is the whole signal. This is the clearest case in the file of a well-evidenced mechanism that we can see the shadow of but cannot measure - and unlike most gaps here, the imbalance feed is a real, purchasable product rather than an exotic one.
falsification_test: First and cheapest: compute mean ES quoted spread by minute for the final 30 minutes of the session versus the session median, over the whole quote sample. This settles whether the 15:45 flatten happens in a cheap or an expensive window and costs one groupby. Second: regress ret_1545_1600 on the day's return, the 15:00-15:45 return and relative volume. Kill the alpha reading unless something is significant at |t| > 2 in both ES and NQ - and note in advance that the lab's own prior finding predicts nothing will be.
cost_feasibility_note: No trades proposed. The value is in re-pricing an existing decision: every session currently ends with a forced round turn at 15:45, and if that minute is systematically more expensive than, say, 15:30 or 16:00, then moving the flatten is a free cost saving applied to 100% of sessions. On ~320 sessions at one forced round turn each, even a quarter-tick of ES spread improvement is 320 x 0.0625 pt x $50 = $1,000 per contract per year, recovered for no added risk and no added trades. That is a better expected return on research effort than most of the directional entries in this file.
why_this_might_be_wrong: I am extrapolating a well-documented CASH EQUITY structural change into index futures without a source that measures the futures side, and the futures market has its own 16:00 settlement conventions and a 17:00 Globex break that may dominate whatever auction-hedging footprint exists. The lab has also already looked at the closing window and found nothing but cost. The honest framing is that the alpha half of this entry is weak and speculative, while the cost half - measure the spread in the minute you are forced to trade in - is nearly certain to be worth its trivial price, and those two halves should not be funded as one item.
